docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Docker is a platform for building, packaging, distributing, and running applications as containers.

A container packages an application together with the dependencies and configuration required to run it, while sharing the host operating system's kernel.

Docker is commonly used for:

  • Local development
  • Application packaging
  • CI/CD
  • Microservices
  • Testing
  • Reproducible environments
  • Deployment
  • Development tooling

docs.title: Docker at a Glance
docs.text:
A typical Docker workflow looks like:

Dockerfile
    │
    │ docker build
    ▼
 Docker Image
    │
    │ docker run
    ▼
 Docker Container
    │
    ├── Volumes
    ├── Networks
    └── Environment variables

For multi-container applications:

             Docker Compose
                   │
       ┌───────────┼───────────┐
       ▼           ▼           ▼
    App           DB          Redis
 Container      Container    Container
       │           │           │
       └───────────┼───────────┘
                   │
               Network

docs.title: Typical Development Workflow
docs.text:
# Build image
docker build -t my-app .

# Run container
docker run -p 8000:8000 my-app

# Check running containers
docker ps

# View logs
docker logs <container>

# Stop container
docker stop <container>

For a Compose project:

docker compose up -d

docs.title: Docker and Git
docs.text:
A Docker project will commonly contain:

project/
├── .git/
├── Dockerfile
├── .dockerignore
├── compose.yaml
├── src/
└── README.md

Docker configuration should normally be committed to Git.

Generated data, secrets, local configuration, and unnecessary build artifacts should not be committed.

docs.title: Docker and CI/CD
docs.text:
Docker is commonly used in CI/CD to:

  1. Build an application image
  2. Run tests
  3. Tag the image
  4. Push it to a registry
  5. Deploy the image

Example:

Git Push
   │
   ▼
CI Pipeline
   │
   ├── Test
   ├── Build
   ├── Scan
   └── Push
         │
         ▼
      Registry
         │
         ▼
      Deployment

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
List images:

or:

docker image ls

Pull an image:

Remove an image:

docs.title: Build Images
docs.text:
Build from the current directory:

docker build -t my-app .

Specify a Dockerfile:

docker build -f Dockerfile.dev -t my-app:dev .

Build with a tag:

docker build -t my-app:1.0 .

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
List running containers:

docker ps

List all containers:

docker ps -a

Run a container:

docker run nginx

Run in the background:

docker run -d nginx

Give the container a name:

docker run -d --name web nginx

Map a port:

docker run -d \
  --name web \
  -p 8080:80 \
  nginx

docs.title: Container Lifecycle
docs.text:
Start:

docker start <container>

Stop:

docker stop <container>

Restart:

docker restart <container>

Remove:

docker rm <container>

Force removal:

docker rm -f <container>

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
View logs:

docker logs <container>

Follow logs:

docker logs -f <container>

Show timestamps:

docker logs -t <container>

docs.title: Execute Commands
docs.text:
Execute a command:

docker exec <container> <command>

Open an interactive shell:

docker exec -it <container> sh

For images containing Bash:

docs.title: Copy Files
docs.text:
Container → host:

docker cp <container>:/path/file .

Host → container:

docker cp ./file <container>:/path/

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Remove stopped containers:

docker container prune

Remove unused images:

docker image prune

Remove unused resources:

docker system prune

Danger

docker system prune can remove unused containers, networks, images, and build cache.

Review what will be removed before using aggressive cleanup commands.

docs.title: Simple Workflow
docs.text:

docker run -d \
  --name web \

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
Docker Compose defines multi-container applications using YAML.

The modern command is:

docker compose

docs.title: Basic Compose File
docs.text:
Create:

compose.yaml

Example:

services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: example

Start:

docker compose up

Background:

docker compose up -d

Stop and remove:

docker compose down

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Each entry under services defines a container/service.

services:
  app:
    image: my-app

  database:
    image: postgres

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
services:
  app:
    build: .

Build:

docker compose build

Build and start:

docker compose up --build

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
ports:
  - "8000:8000"

Format:

host:container

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
services:
  app:
    environment:
      APP_ENV: production
      LOG_LEVEL: info

Use an .env file for local configuration:

APP_ENV=development

docs.title: Volumes
docs.text:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  postgres-data:

docs.title: Networks
docs.text:
services:
  app:
    networks:
      - backend

  db:
    networks:
      - backend

networks:
  backend:

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
services:
  app:
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres

depends_on controls startup ordering but does not by itself guarantee that the dependency is ready to accept connections.

Applications should generally handle connection retries or use appropriate health checks.

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
Example:

services:
  db:
    image: postgres
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Start:

docker compose up

Start detached:

docker compose up -d

Stop:

docker compose stop

Restart:

docker compose restart

View services:

docker compose ps

View logs:

docker compose logs

Follow logs:

docker compose logs -f

View one service:

docker compose logs -f app

Execute command:

docker compose exec app sh

Build:

docker compose build

Pull images:

docker compose pull

Remove application:

docker compose down

Remove volumes too:

docker compose down -v

Danger

docker compose down -v removes the Compose-managed volumes.

This can permanently delete database data.

docs.title: Docker Concepts
docs.text: Understanding the difference between an image, container, volume, network, and registry is fundamental to using Docker effectively.

docs.title: Image
docs.text:
An image is an immutable template used to create containers.

Image
  │
  ├── Application
  ├── Runtime
  ├── Dependencies
  └── Configuration

Images are composed of layers.

docs.title: Container
docs.text:
A container is a running or stopped instance of an image.

Image
  │
  ├── Container A
  ├── Container B
  └── Container C

Multiple containers can be created from the same image.

docs.title: Image vs Container
docs.text: Image Container Template Instance Immutable Has writable layer Used to create containers Runs the application Stored locally/registry Exists on Docker host

docs.title: Dockerfile
docs.text:
A Dockerfile describes how to build an image.

Example:

FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

CMD ["python", "app.py"]

Build:

docker build -t my-app .

docs.title: Registry
docs.text:
A registry stores Docker images.

Examples include:

  • Docker Hub
  • GitHub Container Registry
  • GitLab Container Registry
  • Amazon ECR
  • Google Artifact Registry
  • Azure Container Registry

Typical workflow:

Local Dockerfile
      │
      ▼
    Image
      │
      │ docker push
      ▼
   Registry
      │
      │ docker pull
      ▼
 Other Docker Host

docs.title: Volume
docs.text:
Volumes provide persistent storage outside the container's writable layer.

Container
    │
    ▼
 Volume
    │
    ▼
Persistent data

If a container is deleted, its writable layer disappears.

A volume can remain.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Docker networks allow containers to communicate.

Example:

app ───────► database
 │
 └─────────► redis

Compose automatically creates a network for services unless configured otherwise.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Configuration can be supplied using environment variables:

docker run \
  -e APP_ENV=production \
  my-app

Inside the application:

APP_ENV=production

Avoid putting passwords and secrets directly into Dockerfiles.

docs.title: Docker Daemon
docs.text:
The Docker daemon manages:

  • Containers
  • Images
  • Networks
  • Volumes
  • Builds

The CLI communicates with the Docker daemon.

docker CLI
    │
    ▼
Docker Engine
    │
    ├── Containers
    ├── Images
    ├── Networks
    └── Volumes

docs.title: Docker Layers
docs.text:
Docker images are built from layers.

For example:

Application layer
        │
Dependencies layer
        │
Runtime layer
        │
Base image

Docker can cache unchanged layers, making subsequent builds faster.

docs.title: Ephemeral Containers
docs.text:
Containers should generally be treated as disposable.

Instead of:

Container
    │
    └── Important database data

prefer:

Container
    │
    └── Application

Volume
    │
    └── Database data

This separates application lifecycle from data lifecycle.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text: A container is an isolated process created from a Docker image.

docs.title: Create and Run
docs.text:
docker run nginx

Detached:

docker run -d nginx

Named:

docker run -d --name web nginx

docs.title: Port Mapping
docs.text:
A container port is not automatically accessible from the host.

docker run -d \
  -p 8080:80 \
  nginx

The format is:

host_port:container_port

So:

localhost:8080
      │
      ▼
container:80

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
docker run \
  -e APP_ENV=development \
  my-app

Multiple variables:

docker run \
  -e APP_ENV=production \
  -e LOG_LEVEL=info \
  my-app

docs.title: Container Names
docs.text:
docker run --name web nginx

Then:

docker stop web
docker start web
docker logs web
docker rm web

docs.title: Interactive Containers
docs.text: docker run -it ubuntu bash

docs.title: Detached Containers
docs.text: docker run -d nginx

docs.title: Restart Policies
docs.text:
Always restart:

docker run \
  --restart always \
  nginx

Restart unless explicitly stopped:

docker run \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  nginx

docs.title: Resource Limits
docs.text:
Memory:

docker run \
  --memory 512m \
  my-app

CPU:

docker run \
  --cpus 1 \
  my-app

docs.title: Inspect
docs.text:
docker inspect <container>

Container processes:

docker top <container>

Resource usage:

docker stats

docs.title: Container Lifecycle
docs.text:
Created
   │
   ▼
Running
   │
   ├── stop ──► Stopped
   │
   └── crash ─► Exited
                   │
                   ▼
                 Removed

A stopped container still exists until removed.

docs.title: Container vs VM
docs.text: Container Virtual Machine Shares host kernel Has guest OS/kernel Lightweight Heavier Starts quickly Usually slower Process isolation Hardware/OS virtualization Smaller footprint Larger footprint

docs.title: Dockerfiles
docs.text: A Dockerfile contains instructions used to build a Docker image.

docs.title: Basic Dockerfile
docs.text:
FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["python", "app.py"]

Build:

docker build -t my-app .

Run:

docker run -p 8000:8000 my-app

docs.title: FROM
docs.text:
Defines the base image:

FROM python:3.12-slim

Every normal Dockerfile starts with a base image.

docs.title: WORKDIR
docs.text:
Sets the working directory:

WORKDIR /app

docs.title: COPY
docs.text:
Copies files from the build context:

COPY . .

Prefer copying only what is required where practical.

docs.title: RUN
docs.text:
Executes a command during image construction:

RUN apt-get update

docs.title: ENV
docs.text:
Sets environment variables:

ENV APP_ENV=production

Do not use ENV for secrets.

docs.title: EXPOSE
docs.text:
Documents the port the application listens on:

EXPOSE 8000

It does not publish the port to the host.

Publishing is done with:

docker run -p 8000:8000 my-app

docs.title: CMD
docs.text:
Defines the default command:

CMD ["python", "app.py"]

docs.title: ENTRYPOINT
docs.text:
Defines the executable for the container:

ENTRYPOINT ["python"]

Arguments can then be supplied separately.

docs.title: Use Small Base Images
docs.text:
For example:

FROM python:3.12-slim

rather than unnecessarily large base images.

docs.title: Use .dockerignore
docs.text:
Example:

.git
.venv
__pycache__
*.pyc
.env

docs.title: Avoid Secrets
docs.text:
Do not write:

ENV DATABASE_PASSWORD=mysecret

Secrets should be provided at runtime or through an appropriate secret-management mechanism.

docs.title: Combine Related Package Installation
docs.text:
Instead of unnecessarily creating multiple layers:

RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y curl

use:

RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

docs.title: Multi-stage Builds
docs.text:
Multi-stage builds allow build dependencies to be separated from the final runtime image.

FROM golang:1.24 AS builder

WORKDIR /app

COPY . .

RUN go build -o app .

FROM debian:bookworm-slim

COPY --from=builder /app/app /app

CMD ["/app"]

The final image doesn't need the Go compiler.

docs.title: Build Arguments
docs.text:
ARG APP_VERSION=dev

LABEL version=$APP_VERSION

Build:

docker build \
  --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.0 \
  -t my-app:1.0 .

Do not use build arguments for secrets.

docs.title: Build Context
docs.text:
When running:

docker build .

the current directory becomes the build context.

Docker can only COPY files from within the build context.

Use .dockerignore to prevent unnecessary files from being sent to the builder.

docs.title: Docker Images
docs.text: Docker images are immutable templates used to create containers.

docs.title: List Images
docs.text: docker image ls

docs.title: Pull an Image
docs.text:
docker pull nginx

Specific tag:

docker pull nginx:1.27

Note

Avoid relying on latest in production. Explicit version tags make deployments more predictable.

docs.title: Image Tags
docs.text:
An image reference commonly looks like:

registry/repository:tag

Example:

docker.io/library/nginx:1.27

Private registry:

registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0.0

docs.title: Tag an Image
docs.text:
docker tag my-app:latest my-app:1.0

Tag for a registry:

docker tag my-app:latest registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0

docs.title: Push an Image
docs.text:
Login:

docker login registry.example.com

Push:

docker push registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0

docs.title: Inspect an Image
docs.text:
docker image inspect nginx

Show image history:

docker history nginx

docs.title: Remove an Image
docs.text:
docker image rm nginx

Force:

docker image rm -f nginx

docs.title: Image Digest
docs.text:
Tags can be moved to different image versions.

Digests identify a specific image content.

Example:

nginx@sha256:<digest>

For highly reproducible deployments, immutable digests can be preferable to mutable tags.

docs.text:
Dockerfile
     │
     ▼
docker build
     │
     ▼
   Image
     │
     ├── docker run
     │
     └── docker push
             │
             ▼
          Registry

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Docker installation differs slightly depending on the operating system.

For Linux, Docker Engine is the primary component.

For Windows and macOS, Docker Desktop provides the Docker Engine together with the Docker CLI and supporting components.

docs.title: Ubuntu
docs.text:
The recommended approach is to install Docker Engine from Docker's official APT repository rather than relying on an old distribution package.

Remove conflicting packages if present:

sudo apt remove docker.io docker-doc docker-compose podman-docker containerd runc

Install prerequisites:

sudo apt update

sudo apt install ca-certificates curl

Create the keyring directory:

sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings

Add Docker's signing key:

sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg \
  -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc

sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc

Add the Docker repository:

echo \
  "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc] \
  https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu \
  $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable" | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null

Install Docker:

sudo apt update

sudo apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io \
  docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
Check the Docker version:

docker --version

More detailed information:

docker version

Check the daemon:

sudo systemctl status docker

Run the test image:

sudo docker run hello-world

docs.title: Run Docker Without sudo
docs.text:
By default, Docker's Unix socket is accessible to root.

Add your user to the docker group:

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

Then log out and back in.

Alternatively:

newgrp docker

Test:

docker run hello-world

Danger

Membership of the docker group effectively grants root-level control over the host through Docker.

Only add trusted users to this group.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
The standard approach is Docker Desktop.

Using Homebrew:

brew install --cask docker

Start Docker Desktop from Applications.

Verify:

docker version

Test:

docker run hello-world

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Docker Desktop is the standard installation for Windows.

Using WinGet:

winget install Docker.DockerDesktop

Start Docker Desktop and allow it to configure the required WSL 2 integration if prompted.

Verify from PowerShell:

docker version

Test:

docker run hello-world

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
Modern Docker installations provide Compose as a Docker CLI plugin.

Verify:

docker compose version

Use:

docker compose up

rather than the older:

docker-compose up

Modern syntax

The recommended modern command is:

docker compose

Older installations may use the separate docker-compose command.

docs.title: Docker Networking
docs.text: Docker networking allows containers to communicate with one another and with external systems.

docs.title: List Networks
docs.text:
docker network ls

Inspect:

docker network inspect <network>

docs.title: Default Networks
docs.text:
Docker normally provides networks such as:

bridge
host
none

docs.title: Create a Network
docs.text: docker network create app-network

docs.title: Connect Containers
docs.text:
Run containers on the same network:

docker run -d \
  --name db \
  --network app-network \
  postgres

docker run -d \
  --name app \
  --network app-network \
  my-app

The application can communicate with the database using:

db

as the hostname.

docs.title: Container DNS
docs.text:
Docker provides DNS resolution between containers on user-defined networks.

Example:

app
 │
 │ database connection
 ▼
db:5432

The hostname is the container/service name.

docs.title: Port Publishing
docs.text:
Publish a container port:

docker run \
  -p 8080:80 \
  nginx

This exposes the container's port 80 through host port 8080.

docs.title: Port Binding
docs.text:
Bind only to localhost:

docker run \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 \
  nginx

This prevents direct access through other host interfaces.

docs.title: Network Isolation
docs.text:
Containers on different isolated networks generally cannot communicate directly.

This can be useful for separating application tiers.

Example:

frontend-network
      │
      ▼
   frontend

backend-network
      │
      ├── API
      └── Database

docs.title: Compose Networking
docs.text:
Docker Compose creates a project network automatically.

Example:

services:
  app:
    image: my-app

  db:
    image: postgres

The application can connect to:

db:5432

rather than using localhost.

Warning

Inside a container, localhost refers to the current container, not another container and not necessarily the host machine.

docs.title: Docker Registries
docs.text: A Docker registry stores and distributes container images.

docs.title: Common Registries
docs.text: Registry Example Docker Hub docker.io/user/app GitHub Container Registry ghcr.io/user/app GitLab Container Registry registry.gitlab.com/group/project Amazon ECR <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/app Google Artifact Registry <region>-docker.pkg.dev/... Azure Container Registry <registry>.azurecr.io/app

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
Docker Hub:

docker login

Private registry:

docker login registry.example.com

docs.title: Tag an Image
docs.text:
docker tag my-app:latest \
  registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0.0

docs.title: Push
docs.text:
docker push \
  registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0.0

docs.title: Pull
docs.text:
docker pull \
  registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0.0

docs.title: Complete Workflow
docs.text:
docker build -t my-app:1.0.0 .

docker login registry.example.com

docker tag my-app:1.0.0 \
  registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0.0

docker push \
  registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0.0

On another machine:

docker login registry.example.com

docker pull \
  registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0.0

docs.title: Image Naming
docs.text:
A complete image reference can contain:

registry/repository:tag

Example:

registry.example.com/team/backend:1.4.2

Components:

registry.example.com
        │
        └── Registry

team/backend
        │
        └── Repository

1.4.2
        │
        └── Tag

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Common release tags:

1.0.0
1.0
1
latest

For production deployments, immutable version tags or digests are preferable to mutable tags such as latest.

docs.title: Image Digests
docs.text:
A digest identifies specific image content:

my-app@sha256:<digest>

This allows deployments to reference an exact image rather than relying on a mutable tag.

docs.title: Docker Security
docs.text:
Docker containers provide process and filesystem isolation, but they are not automatically secure simply because they are containers.

Security should be considered at the image, container, host, network, registry, and secret-management levels.

docs.title: Run as a Non-root User
docs.text:
Avoid running applications as root where possible.

Dockerfile:

RUN useradd --create-home appuser

USER appuser

docs.title: Use Trusted Base Images
docs.text:
Prefer:

  • Official images
  • Verified publishers
  • Minimal images
  • Pinned versions
  • Regularly updated images

Avoid blindly using arbitrary images from public registries.

docs.title: Don't Store Secrets in Images
docs.text:
Never do:

ENV API_KEY=secret-value

or:

COPY .env /app/.env

Secrets can remain in image layers even if later deleted.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Environment variables are useful for configuration:

docker run \
  -e APP_ENV=production \
  my-app

But environment variables are not always an appropriate secret-management mechanism.

For sensitive production secrets, use a proper secret-management solution.

docs.title: Read-only Filesystem
docs.text:
Where possible:

docker run \
  --read-only \
  my-app

If temporary storage is required, provide an explicit writable location.

docs.title: Drop Capabilities
docs.text:
Linux capabilities can be reduced:

docker run \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  my-app

Only add required capabilities.

docs.title: Avoid Privileged Containers
docs.text:
Avoid:

docker run --privileged ...

unless there is a well-understood requirement.

Privileged containers significantly increase the container's access to the host.

docs.title: Resource Limits
docs.text:
Limit resources to reduce denial-of-service risk:

docker run \
  --memory 512m \
  --cpus 1 \
  my-app

docs.title: Network Exposure
docs.text:
Don't expose ports unnecessarily.

Instead of:

-p 8080:80

consider:

-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80

when the service should only be accessible locally.

docs.title: Image Scanning
docs.text:
Images should be scanned for known vulnerabilities.

The exact scanning tool depends on your environment and CI/CD platform.

A typical workflow is:

Build
  │
  ▼
Scan
  │
  ├── PASS ──► Push
  │
  └── FAIL ──► Fix

docs.title: .dockerignore
docs.text:
Prevent secrets and unnecessary files from entering the build context:

.git
.env
.venv
__pycache__
*.pem
*.key

docs.title: Docker Socket
docs.text:
Be extremely careful with:

/var/run/docker.sock

Giving a container access to the Docker socket can effectively give it control over the Docker host.

Avoid mounting it unless absolutely necessary.

docs.title: Security Checklist
docs.text:
• Use trusted base images
  • Keep images updated
  • Run as non-root
  • Avoid --privileged
  • Drop unnecessary capabilities
  • Minimize exposed ports
  • Don't bake secrets into images
  • Use .dockerignore
  • Scan images
  • Apply resource limits
  • Protect the Docker socket
  • Use immutable image references where appropriate
  • Keep Docker Engine and Docker Desktop updated

docs.title: Docker Troubleshooting
docs.text:
A useful Docker troubleshooting process is:

Problem
  │
  ├── Container running?
  ├── Image correct?
  ├── Logs?
  ├── Network?
  ├── Ports?
  ├── Environment?
  ├── Volumes?
  └── Resources?

docs.title: Docker Daemon Not Running
docs.text:
Check:

docker info

Linux:

sudo systemctl status docker

Start:

sudo systemctl start docker

Enable at boot:

sudo systemctl enable docker

docs.title: Permission Denied
docs.text:
If you see:

permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket

Check:

groups

Add your user:

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

Then log out and back in.

docs.title: Container Exits Immediately
docs.text:
Check:

docker ps -a

Then:

docker logs <container>

Inspect:

docker inspect <container>

The most common cause is that the container's main process has exited.

docs.title: Container Keeps Restarting
docs.text:
Check:

docker ps

Then:

docker logs <container>

Inspect restart configuration:

docker inspect <container>

Look for application crashes, configuration errors, failed health checks, or missing dependencies.

docs.title: Port Already in Use
docs.text:
If Docker reports:

Bind for 0.0.0.0:8080 failed: port is already allocated

Find what is using the port on Linux:

sudo ss -ltnp | grep :8080

Or change the host port:

docker run \
  -p 8081:80 \
  nginx

docs.title: Container Cannot Reach Another Container
docs.text:
Check the networks:

docker network ls

Inspect:

docker network inspect <network>

Ensure both containers are connected to the same user-defined network.

Within Compose, use the service name:

db:5432

not:

localhost:5432

docs.title: Container Cannot Reach Internet
docs.text:
Check:

docker exec -it <container> sh

Then test DNS:

getent hosts example.com

Check network configuration:

docker inspect <container>

docs.title: Image Won't Build
docs.text:
Build without relying on cache:

docker build --no-cache -t my-app .

Use verbose build output:

docker build --progress=plain -t my-app .

Check:

  • Dockerfile syntax
  • Build context
  • .dockerignore
  • Package repositories
  • Network connectivity
  • Base image availability

docs.title: File Not Found During COPY
docs.text:
If:

COPY something.txt /app/

fails, verify that the file exists inside the build context.

For:

docker build .

Docker can only access files below the current build context.

Check .dockerignore.

docs.title: Container Has No Data
docs.text:
Check mounts:

docker inspect <container>

Look under:

Mounts

List volumes:

docker volume ls

Inspect:

docker volume inspect <volume>

docs.title: Check Resource Usage
docs.text:
docker stats

Check disk usage:

docker system df

docs.title: Clean Up Disk Space
docs.text:
Unused containers:

docker container prune

Unused images:

docker image prune

Unused networks:

docker network prune

Unused volumes:

docker volume prune

General cleanup:

docker system prune

Danger

Cleanup commands can delete resources you may still need.

docs.title: Compose Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Check configuration:

docker compose config

List services:

docker compose ps

View logs:

docker compose logs

Follow logs:

docker compose logs -f

Rebuild:

docker compose build --no-cache

Restart:

docker compose down
docker compose up -d

docs.title: Useful Diagnostic Sequence
docs.text:
When a container isn't working:

docker ps -a

docker logs <container>

docker inspect <container>

docker stats

docker network ls

docker volume ls

For Compose:

docker compose ps

docker compose logs

docker compose config

docker compose images

This usually narrows the problem down to one of:

Image
  │
  ├── Build problem
  ├── Configuration
  ├── Application
  ├── Networking
  ├── Storage
  ├── Permissions
  └── Resources

docs.title: Docker Volumes
docs.text:
Containers are ephemeral (lasting for short time) by design.

If application data needs to survive container replacement, use persistent storage.

docs.title: Named Volumes
docs.text:
Create:

docker volume create app-data

List:

docker volume ls

Inspect:

docker volume inspect app-data

Remove:

docker volume rm app-data

docs.title: Mount a Volume
docs.text:
docker run \
  -v app-data:/data \
  my-app

Format:

volume_name:container_path

docs.title: Bind Mount
docs.text:
A host directory can be mounted:

docker run \
  -v $(pwd)/data:/data \
  my-app

This is useful for development.

docs.title: Read-only Mount
docs.text:
docker run \
  -v $(pwd)/config:/config:ro \
  my-app

docs.title: Volume vs Bind Mount
docs.text: Volume Bind Mount Managed by Docker Managed by user Docker storage location Explicit host path Good for persistent application data Good for development/source code Easier to move/manage Direct host filesystem access

docs.title: Database Example
docs.text:
docker volume create postgres-data

docker run -d \
  --name postgres \
  -v postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres

Deleting the container:

docker rm -f postgres

does not delete the volume.

The data remains in:

postgres-data

docs.title: Volume Cleanup
docs.text:
List volumes:

docker volume ls

Remove unused volumes:

docker volume prune

Danger

Removing a volume permanently removes the data stored in that volume.

Ensure backups exist before deleting production volumes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Git is a distributed version control system (VCS) used to track changes to files, manage branches, and collaborate with other developers.

What does distributed mean?

Git is distributed, meaning each developer typically has a complete copy of the repository and its history on their local machine.

  • Git allows developers to:

    • Track changes to files over time.
    • Create and manage different versions of a project.
    • Work on multiple features using branches.
    • Collaborate with other developers.
    • Revert changes when something goes wrong.
    • Merge work from different developers.
    • Maintain a complete history of a project.

docs.title: How Git Is Used
docs.text:
A typical Git workflow moves changes through several stages:

flowchart LR
    A["Working Directory"] -->|"git add"| B["Staging Area"]
    B -->|"git commit"| C["Local Repository"]
    C -->|"git push"| D["Remote Repository"]
    D -->|"git pull"| A

docs.title: Git Jargon
docs.text: Term Meaning Repository (repo) A Git-managed project containing files and their complete version history. Working directory The checked-out files on your computer that you can edit. Staging area (index) The changes selected for inclusion in the next commit. Commit A recorded snapshot of staged changes. Branch A movable pointer to a line of development. HEAD A reference to the currently checked-out commit, usually the tip of the current branch. Main branch The primary branch of a repository, commonly named main. Remote A reference to another Git repository, usually hosted on a server. Origin The conventional name for the remote repository created when cloning. Upstream The remote branch that a local branch is configured to track. Clone A local copy of a remote repository, including its history. Fetch Downloads information from a remote without integrating it into the current branch. Pull Fetches changes from a remote and integrates them into the current branch. Push Uploads local commits to a remote repository. Merge Combines the histories of two branches. Merge commit A commit created when Git merges two diverging branches. Fast-forward A merge where the target branch moves forward without creating a merge commit. Rebase Replays commits onto a different base commit, creating new commit objects. Conflict A situation where Git cannot automatically combine changes. Tag A named reference to a specific commit, commonly used to mark releases. Stash Temporary storage for uncommitted changes. Working tree Another term for the checked-out files in the working directory. Tracked file A file that Git monitors for changes. Untracked file A file that Git is not yet monitoring. Index Git's internal representation of the staging area. SHA / commit hash An identifier used to reference a Git object, such as a commit. Repository history The sequence of commits recording how a project has changed over time.

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
A typical Git workflow is:

flowchart LR
    A[Working Directory] -->|git add| B[Staging Area]
    B -->|git commit| C[Local Repository]
    C -->|git push| D[Remote Repository]
    D -->|git fetch / pull| C

The three main local areas are:

Area Description Working directory Files currently being edited Staging area Changes selected for the next commit Repository Committed project history

Tip

Think of git add as preparing changes and git commit as recording those prepared changes in Git history.

docs.title: Branching
docs.text:
Branches allow development to happen independently.

Why use branches?

Branches allow you to develop features, fixes, or experiments without making changes directly on the main branch.

docs.title: List Branches
docs.text:
git branch

Include remote branches:

git branch -a

docs.title: Create a Branch
docs.text: git branch feature/login

docs.title: Switch
docs.text: git switch feature/login

docs.title: Checkout
docs.text: git checkout feature/login

docs.title: New Syntax
docs.text: git switch -c feature/login

docs.title: Older Syntax
docs.text: git checkout -b feature/login

docs.title: Delete a Branch
docs.text:
git branch -d feature/login

Force deletion:

git branch -D feature/login

docs.title: Rename a Branch
docs.text:
git branch -m new-name

Rename the current branch to main:

git branch -m main

Tip

Prefer git switch for branch operations. It makes the intent clearer than the older multi-purpose git checkout command.

docs.title: Command Table
docs.text:
Command What it does git init Creates a new Git repository git clone <url> Copies a remote repository to your computer git status Shows the current state of the working directory git add <file> Stages a file for the next commit git add . Stages all changes in the current directory git commit -m "message" Creates a commit containing staged changes git log Displays the commit history git diff Shows changes that have not been staged git branch Lists or manages branches git switch <branch> Switches to another branch git switch -c <branch> Creates and switches to a new branch git checkout <branch> Older syntax: switches to another branch git checkout -b <branch> Older syntax: creates and switches to a new branch git merge <branch> Merges another branch into the current branch git remote -v Displays configured remote repositories git fetch Downloads changes from a remote without merging them git pull Downloads and integrates changes from a remote repository git push Uploads local commits to a remote repository git restore <file> Restores a file to a previous state git checkout -- <file> Older syntax: restores a file to its last committed state git rm <file> Removes a file and stages its deletion git mv <old> <new> Moves or renames a file and stages the change git reset Moves the current branch or changes staging state git tag <name> Creates a tag for a specific commit

Command syntax

Values written inside <angle-brackets> are placeholders. Replace them with the value appropriate for your repository.

Modern vs. older Git syntax

git switch and git restore were introduced to separate two different jobs that were historically handled by git checkout.

Modern:

  • git switch <branch> → switch branches
  • git switch -c <branch> → create and switch branches
  • git restore <file> → restore files

Older:

  • git checkout <branch> → switch branches
  • git checkout -b <branch> → create and switch branches
  • git checkout -- <file> → restore files

You will still encounter git checkout frequently in older documentation, scripts, and tutorials.

docs.title: Simple Workflow
docs.text: A basic workflow for making and committing changes to a Git repository looks like this:

docs.title: 1. Create a repository
docs.text: git init

docs.title: 2. Check the repository status
docs.text: git status

docs.title: 4. Review your changes
docs.text: git diff

docs.title: 5. Stage the changes
docs.text: git add .

docs.title: 6. Check what will be committed
docs.text: git status

docs.title: 7. Create a commit
docs.text: git commit -m "Add initial files"

docs.title: 8. View the commit history
docs.text: git log

docs.title: 9. Push changes to repository
docs.text:
git push

The basic cycle is:

Edit → Diff → Add → Commit → Push

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Git configuration is stored at different levels:

Level Scope Command System All users git config --system Global Current user git config --global Local Current repository git config --local

docs.title: User Identity
docs.text:
Configure the name associated with commits:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"

Configure the email:

git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

Check the configuration:

git config --global --list

docs.title: Default Branch
docs.text:
Set the default initial branch name:

git config --global init.defaultBranch main

docs.title: Editor
docs.text:
Configure the default Git editor:

git config --global core.editor vim

docs.title: Useful Configuration
docs.text:
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.autocrlf input
git config --global pull.rebase false

Tip

Repository-specific configuration overrides global configuration.

docs.title: Diffs
docs.text: git diff shows differences between versions of your files.

docs.title: Working Directory vs Staging
docs.text:
git diff

Shows unstaged changes.

docs.title: Staging vs Last Commit
docs.text:
git diff --staged

Also:

git diff --cached

docs.title: Compare Commits
docs.text: git diff <commit1> <commit2>

docs.title: Compare Branches
docs.text: git diff main feature/login

docs.title: Diff a Specific File
docs.text: git diff -- path/to/file

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
git diff --stat

Note

git diff by itself does not show changes that have already been staged. Use git diff --staged to inspect the staging area.

Useful review step

Reviewing git diff --staged before committing lets you verify exactly what will be included in the commit.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
After installing Git, the next step is to authenticate with GitHub and connect a local project to a GitHub repository.

There are two common ways to authenticate Git with GitHub:

Method Recommended for Authentication HTTPS + GitHub CLI Most developers Browser-based authentication SSH Developers who prefer SSH keys SSH key pair

Recommended setup

For a new development machine, GitHub CLI + HTTPS is a simple option. GitHub CLI can authenticate through the browser and store the credentials used by Git.

docs.title: 1. Authenticate with GitHub
docs.text:
Verify Git

Before installing GitHub CLI, verify that Git is installed:

git --version

Example:

git version 2.51.0

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
The installation method depends on your Linux distribution.

Debian / Ubuntu

For Debian and Ubuntu systems, GitHub provides an apt installation method.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install gh

Verify the installation: 

gh --version

Example:

gh version 2.x.x

Fedora / RHEL

On Fedora and compatible RHEL-based distributions:

sudo dnf install gh

Then:

gh --version

GitHub lists dnf as the installation method for Fedora/RHEL systems.

openSUSE / SUSE

For openSUSE and SUSE systems:

sudo zypper install gh

Then:

gh --version

GitHub also provides package downloads for distributions where a package manager is not available.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
Homebrew

The simplest method on macOS is Homebrew:

brew install gh

Verify:

gh --version

GitHub officially documents Homebrew as the macOS installation method.

If Homebrew is not installed, you can install it separately, then run:

brew install gh

Tip

If you already use Homebrew for development tools such as Git, Python, Node.js, Docker, or Terraform, installing gh through Homebrew keeps your command-line tooling in one package manager.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
WinGet

On modern Windows installations, the easiest terminal-based installation is Windows Package Manager:

winget install --id GitHub.cli

After installation, open a new terminal and verify:

gh --version

GitHub lists WinGet as the Windows package-manager installation method.

Windows Terminal

If you're using Windows Terminal, PowerShell, or Command Prompt:

gh --version

should work after installation.

Note

If gh is not recognised immediately after installation, close and reopen your terminal so that the updated PATH is loaded.

Verify the Installation

Regardless of operating system:

gh --version

You can also display the available commands:

gh help

For example: 

gh auth
gh repo
gh pr
gh issue
gh workflow

  • gh auth is particularly important because it is used to authenticate your GitHub account.

docs.title: 2. Verify Git Installation
docs.text:
Check that Git is installed:

git --version

Example:

git version 2.51.0

Configure your Git identity:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

Check the configuration:

git config --global --list

Git identity vs GitHub authentication

user.name and user.email identify the author of your commits.

They do not authenticate you with GitHub.

GitHub authentication determines whether you are allowed to clone, pull, or push to a repository.

docs.title: Option A — GitHub CLI + HTTPS
docs.text:
Install the GitHub CLI (gh) for your operating system.

Verify it:

gh --version

Authenticate:

gh auth login

Follow the prompts.

Choose:

? What account do you want to log into?
> GitHub.com

? What is your preferred protocol for Git operations?
> HTTPS

? Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials?
> Yes

? How would you like to authenticate GitHub CLI?
> Login with a web browser

GitHub CLI will provide a one-time code and open a browser where you can authenticate to your GitHub account.

Check your authentication:

gh auth status

You should see information indicating that you are logged into GitHub.

Tip

With HTTPS authentication through GitHub CLI, you do not need to manually create and copy a personal access token for normal Git operations. GitHub CLI can store the Git credentials for you.

docs.title: Option B — SSH Authentication
docs.text:
SSH is another common way to authenticate with GitHub.

Check whether you already have an SSH key:

ls ~/.ssh

Look for files such as:

id_ed25519
id_ed25519.pub

If you don't have a key, create one:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"

Start the SSH agent:

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

Add your private key:

ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Display your public key:

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Copy the entire output.

In GitHub, add the public key under:

Settings
→ SSH and GPG keys
→ New SSH key

GitHub requires the public key to be added to your account before the SSH key can authenticate you.

Test the connection:

ssh -T git@github.com

A successful authentication will produce a message indicating that GitHub has successfully authenticated your account.

Never share your private key

Never upload or share:

~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Only the .pub file should be added to GitHub.

docs.title: 3. Create a Repository on GitHub
docs.text:
Create a new repository on GitHub.

For example:

Repository name: my-project

You will then have a remote repository such as:

https://github.com/<username>/my-project.git

or:

git@github.com:<username>/my-project.git

GitHub supports both HTTPS and SSH remote URLs.

Empty repository

If you already have a local project that you want to push to GitHub, creating an **empty GitHub repository** is often the simplest approach.

docs.title: 4. Connect Your Local IDE Project
docs.text:
Open your project directory in your IDE.

For example:

cd ~/projects/my-project

You can use any IDE, such as VS Code, IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, or another Git-compatible editor.

The IDE is simply working with the Git repository on your filesystem.

The important relationship is:

IDE
 │
 │ edits files
 ▼
Local Git Repository
 │
 │ git push
 ▼
GitHub Repository

docs.title: 5. Initialize the Local Repository
docs.text:
If the project does not already contain a Git repository:

git init

This creates a hidden .git directory:

my-project/
├── .git/
├── src/
├── README.md
└── ...

Check the repository:

git status

You should see the files listed as untracked files.

Note

git init creates the local repository. It does not connect the repository to GitHub yet.

docs.title: 6. Create a .gitignore
docs.text:
Before committing your files, create a .gitignore file.

For example:

# IDE
.vscode/
.idea/

# Environment variables
.env
.env.*

# Python
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/

# Node
node_modules/

# Build output
dist/
build/

The .gitignore prevents files such as secrets, dependencies, IDE configuration, and build artifacts from being committed.

Danger

Never commit secrets such as:

.env
API keys
passwords
private SSH keys
cloud credentials

docs.title: 7. Stage the Project
docs.text:
Check what Git sees:

git status

Stage the files:

git add .

Check the staging area:

git status

You should now see the files under:

Changes to be committed

docs.title: 8. Create the First Commit
docs.text:
Create your initial commit:

git commit -m "Initial commit"

Check the history:

git log --oneline

Example:

a1b2c3d (HEAD -> main) Initial commit

At this point:

Working Directory
        │
        │ git add
        ▼
Staging Area
        │
        │ git commit
        ▼
Local Repository

The repository is still only local.

docs.title: 9. Connect the Repository to GitHub
docs.text: Add the GitHub repository as a remote:

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text: git remote add origin https://github.com/<username>/my-project.git

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
git remote add origin git@github.com:<username>/my-project.git

Check the remote:

git remote -v

Example:

origin  https://github.com/<username>/my-project.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/<username>/my-project.git (push)

origin is simply the conventional name Git gives to the primary remote repository.

docs.title: 10. Set the Main Branch
docs.text:
Modern repositories commonly use main as the primary branch.

Set your local branch to main:

git branch -M main

Check:

git branch

You should see:

* main

docs.title: 11. Push the Repository to GitHub
docs.text:
Push the local main branch:

git push -u origin main

The -u option establishes the upstream relationship between your local branch and the remote branch.

After this, future pushes can usually be performed with:

git push

The complete relationship is now:

Local main
    │
    │ git push
    ▼
origin/main
    │
    ▼
GitHub

docs.title: 12. Verify the Remote
docs.text:
Check the configured remote:

git remote -v

Check the branch tracking relationship:

git branch -vv

Example:

* main a1b2c3d [origin/main] Initial commit

This means your local main branch is tracking origin/main.

docs.title: 13. Normal Development Workflow
docs.text:
Once everything is configured, your normal workflow becomes:

# Check current state
git status

# Create a branch for your work
git switch -c feature/my-change

# Edit files
# ...

# Review changes
git diff

# Stage changes
git add .

# Commit changes
git commit -m "Add my change"

# Push branch to GitHub
git push -u origin feature/my-change

The workflow is:

                    GitHub
                       ▲
                       │
                    git push
                       │
                       │
IDE → Working Tree → Staging → Local Commit
        │               │           │
        │            git add     git commit
        │
      edit

docs.title: 14. Connecting an Existing Local Project
docs.text:
If you already have a project:

my-project/
├── src/
├── README.md
├── package.json
└── ...

You can connect it directly:

cd my-project

git init

git branch -M main

git add .

git commit -m "Initial commit"

git remote add origin https://github.com/<username>/my-project.git

git push -u origin main

For SSH:

git remote add origin git@github.com:<username>/my-project.git

docs.title: 15. Cloning an Existing GitHub Repository
docs.text:
If the repository already exists on GitHub and you want to work on it locally, you normally do not use git init.

Instead, clone it:

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text: git clone https://github.com/<username>/my-project.git

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:<username>/my-project.git

Then:

cd my-project

Open the directory in your IDE.

For example, with VS Code:

code .

Check the repository:

git status

You can then make changes, commit, and push:

git add .
git commit -m "Update project"
git push

Clone vs init

Use:

```bash
git clone <url>
```

when the repository **already exists remotely**.

Use:

```bash
git init
```

when you have an **existing local project** that you want to turn into a Git repository.

docs.title: 16. GitHub Authentication vs Repository Connection
docs.text:
These are two separate steps:

1. Authenticate
       │
       ▼
   GitHub knows
   who you are
       │
       ▼
2. Configure remote
       │
       ▼
   Git knows where
   the repository is
       │
       ▼
3. Push / Pull

For example:

gh auth login

handles authentication.

While:

git remote add origin https://github.com/<username>/my-project.git

connects your local Git repository to the GitHub repository.

Note

Authentication does not automatically connect your project to a repository.

Likewise, adding a remote does not grant you permission to push. You need both a correctly configured remote and valid authentication/authorization.

Create commit git commit -m "message" Add GitHub remote git remote add origin <url> Check remote git remote -v Rename branch to main git branch -M main Push first time git push -u origin main Push subsequent changes git push Download remote changes git pull

docs.title: Complete First-Time Setup
docs.text:
For an existing local project, the entire process can be reduced to:

# Authenticate with GitHub
gh auth login

# Configure Git identity
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

# Go to your project
cd my-project

# Initialize Git
git init

# Use main as the primary branch
git branch -M main

# Stage and commit
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"

# Connect to GitHub
git remote add origin https://github.com/<username>/my-project.git

# Push to GitHub
git push -u origin main

After the initial setup:

git add .
git commit -m "Describe your change"
git push

That's the basic IDE → Git → GitHub workflow.

Recommended mental model

Remember the difference between these four things:

`text GitHub Account │ │ authentication ▼ GitHub Access │ │ remote URL ▼ Local Git Repository │ │ edited by ▼ IDE / Working Directory Your IDE does not need a separate Git repository. It works with the .git repository in your project directory and uses Git's configured authentication to communicate with GitHub.

docs.title: View History
docs.text:
git log

Compact format:

git log --oneline

Graph view:

git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

docs.title: Show a Commit
docs.text: git show <commit>

docs.title: Search Commit Messages
docs.text: git log --grep="keyword"

docs.title: Show a Specific File's History
docs.text: git log -- path/to/file

docs.title: Show Who Changed Each Line
docs.text:
git blame <file>

Tip

A useful general-purpose history command is:

git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

It provides a compact view of commits, branches, and tags.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
On Debian/Ubuntu:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install git

Verify the installation:

git --version

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
Using Homebrew:

brew install git

Verify:

git --version

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Git can be installed using the official Git installer or through a package manager such as winget.

Using winget:

winget install --id Git.Git

Verify:

git --version

docs.title: Verify Git
docs.text:
After installation:

git --version

Example:

git version 2.x.x

Note

The exact version depends on your operating system and installation source.

docs.title: Merging
docs.text: Merging combines changes from one branch into another.

docs.title: Basic Merge
docs.text:
First switch to the branch that should receive the changes:

git switch main

Then merge:

git merge feature/login

docs.title: Fast-Forward Merge
docs.text:
If the target branch has not diverged:

main
  \
   feature

Git can simply move the branch pointer forward.

docs.title: Merge Commit
docs.text:
When branches have diverged, Git may create a merge commit:

A---B---C---M  main
     \     /
      D---E

docs.title: Abort a Merge
docs.text:
If conflicts occur and you want to cancel the merge:

git merge --abort

docs.title: Resolve Conflicts
docs.text:
Git attempts to combine the histories automatically. If the same part of a file has conflicting changes, Git may require you to resolve a merge conflict manually.

Merge conflicts

A merge conflict is not an error in Git. It means Git needs you to decide which changes should be kept before the merge can be completed.

Check conflicted files:

git status

After resolving a file:

git add <file>

Complete the merge:

git commit

docs.title: Remote Repositories
docs.text: Remote repositories allow Git repositories to be shared between machines and developers.

docs.title: List Remotes
docs.text: git remote -v

docs.title: Add a Remote
docs.text: git remote add origin <url>

docs.title: Change a Remote URL
docs.text: git remote set-url origin <url>

docs.title: Fetch Changes
docs.text:
Downloads information about changes from a remote repository without automatically integrating those changes into your current branch.

This is useful when you want to inspect remote changes before deciding whether to merge or otherwise integrate them.

git fetch

Fetch a specific remote:

git fetch origin

docs.title: Pull Changes
docs.text:
git pull

Equivalent conceptually to:

git fetch
git merge

docs.title: Push Changes
docs.text:
Uploads local commits to a remote repository.

git push

When pushing a new branch for the first time:

git push -u origin feature-login

Push a branch and establish its upstream:

The -u option establishes an upstream relationship, making future git push and git pull commands simpler.

git push -u origin main

After the upstream has been configured:

git push

docs.title: Clone a Repository
docs.text:
git clone <url>

Clone into a specific directory:

git clone <url> <directory>

Copies an existing remote repository.

git clone https://github.com/example/my-project.git

Then move into the repository:

cd my-project

Clone vs. init

Use git clone when a repository already exists remotely. Use git init when you are starting a new repository locally.

Note

git fetch downloads remote information without changing your current branch. git pull fetches and then integrates the changes.

docs.title: Staging & Commits
docs.text: Git separates editing files from recording changes.

docs.title: Check Status
docs.text: git status

docs.title: Stage a File
docs.text: git add file.txt

docs.title: Stage Multiple Files
docs.text: git add file1.txt file2.txt

docs.title: Stage Everything
docs.text:
git add .

Or:

git add -A

Review before committing

Use git status after staging to confirm that the intended files are in the staging area.

git status

Git can report:

  • Modified files
  • Untracked files
  • Staged changes
  • The current branch
  • Whether your branch is ahead of or behind its remote branch

docs.title: Commit
docs.text:
git commit -m "Add configuration"

ood commit messages briefly describe what the commit changes.

Examples:

git commit -m "Fix navigation links"
git commit -m "Add installation instructions"
git commit -m "Update API documentation"

Keep commits focused

Small, focused commits are generally easier to review, understand, and revert.

docs.title: Stage and Commit Tracked Files
docs.text:
git commit -am "Update configuration"

Warning

git commit -am does not include new, untracked files. New files must be staged with git add first.

docs.title: Amend the Last Commit
docs.text:
git commit --amend

Change only the commit message:

git commit --amend -m "Correct message"

Danger

Avoid amending commits that have already been shared with other developers unless you understand the consequences of rewriting history.

docs.title: Stash
docs.text: git stash temporarily stores uncommitted changes so you can work on a clean working directory.

docs.title: Stash Changes
docs.text:
git stash

Include untracked files:

git stash -u

docs.title: List Stashes
docs.text: git stash list

docs.title: Apply a Stash
docs.text:
git stash apply

Apply a specific stash:

git stash apply stash@{1}

docs.title: Apply and Remove
docs.text: git stash pop

docs.title: Delete a Stash
docs.text: git stash drop stash@{0}

docs.title: Delete All Stashes
docs.text: git stash clear

docs.title: Named Stash
docs.text:
git stash push -m "Work in progress"

Tip

git stash pop applies the stash and removes it from the stash list. git stash apply leaves the stash available.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: Tags are references to specific commits and are commonly used to identify releases.

docs.title: List Tags
docs.text: git tag

docs.title: Create a Tag
docs.text: git tag v1.0.0

docs.title: Annotated Tag
docs.text: git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release v1.0.0"

docs.title: Show a Tag
docs.text: git show v1.0.0

docs.title: Push a Tag
docs.text:
git push origin v1.0.0

Push all tags:

git push origin --tags

docs.title: Delete a Tag
docs.text:
Local:

git tag -d v1.0.0

Remote:

git push origin --delete v1.0.0

Tip

Annotated tags are generally preferred for releases because they contain metadata such as the tagger, date, and message.

docs.title: Undoing Changes
docs.text: Git provides several ways to undo changes. The correct command depends on where the change currently exists and whether the commit has already been shared with others.

docs.title: Finding HEAD
docs.text:
HEAD refers to the commit currently checked out.

To display the current commit hash:

git rev-parse HEAD

Example:

a1b2c3d4e5f6789012345678901234567890abcd

To display the shortened commit hash:

git rev-parse --short HEAD

Example:

a1b2c3d

You can also see HEAD as part of the commit history:

git log --oneline --decorate -5

Example:

a1b2c3d (HEAD -> main) Add documentation
7f8e9a0 Add Git commands
3c4d5e6 Initial commit

Here, HEAD -> main means that HEAD currently points to the latest commit on the main branch.

docs.title: Finding a Specific Commit
docs.text:
To find the commit hash you want to revert or reset to:

git log --oneline

Example:

a1b2c3d Add new feature
7f8e9a0 Update configuration
3c4d5e6 Initial commit

The shortened hash can generally be used when referring to a commit:

git revert 7f8e9a0

or:

git reset 7f8e9a0

Tip

You usually do not need to copy the entire 40-character commit hash. A sufficiently unique shortened hash, such as 7f8e9a0, is normally enough.

docs.title: Discard Working Directory Changes
docs.text:
Modern syntax:

git restore <file>

This discards uncommitted changes to the specified file and restores it to the version in the index.

Older syntax:

git checkout -- <file>

Warning

These commands discard the file's current uncommitted changes. Make sure you do not need them before running the command.

docs.title: Unstage a File
docs.text:
Remove a file from the staging area while keeping its changes in the working directory:

git restore --staged <file>

The changes are not deleted; they are simply removed from the staging area.

docs.title: Revert a Commit
docs.text:
git revert creates a new commit that reverses the changes introduced by an existing commit.

git revert <commit>

For example:

git revert 7f8e9a0

This is generally the safest approach for commits that have already been pushed to a shared remote repository because it does not rewrite existing history.

Example:

A---B---C---D
        ^
        |
     revert C

A---B---C---D---E
                ^
                |
          E reverses C

Tip

Use git revert when you want to undo a commit while preserving the existing project history.

docs.title: Reset to a Specific Commit
docs.text:
git reset moves the current branch to a different commit.

For example:

git reset <commit>

To move the current branch back to a specific commit:

git reset 7f8e9a0

The effect depends on the reset mode.

docs.title: Soft Reset
docs.text:
Keeps changes staged:

git reset --soft <commit>

Example:

git reset --soft 7f8e9a0

The branch moves to the specified commit, but the changes between the old HEAD and the target commit remain staged.

docs.title: Mixed Reset
docs.text:
Keeps changes in the working directory but unstages them:

git reset --mixed <commit>

This is the default:

git reset <commit>

Example:

git reset 7f8e9a0

The branch moves to the specified commit and the changes remain in the working directory as unstaged changes.

docs.title: Hard Reset
docs.text:
Moves the branch to the specified commit and discards changes from the working directory and staging area:

git reset --hard <commit>

Example:

git reset --hard 7f8e9a0

Danger

git reset --hard can permanently discard uncommitted changes. Use it carefully.

docs.title: Reset Current Branch to HEAD
docs.text:
You can use HEAD as a reference instead of specifying a commit hash.

Unstage all staged changes:

git reset HEAD

Discard all local changes and return the working tree to HEAD:

git reset --hard HEAD

Warning

git reset --hard HEAD discards all uncommitted changes in tracked files.

docs.title: Reset to the Previous Commit
docs.text:
Git supports relative references such as HEAD~1.

Move the current branch back one commit:

git reset --hard HEAD~1

Two commits:

git reset --hard HEAD~2

For example:

A---B---C---D  HEAD
        ^
        |
      HEAD~1

Here:

  • HEAD → D
  • HEAD~1 → C
  • HEAD~2 → B
  • HEAD~3 → A

Danger

A hard reset changes the branch history. Avoid using it on commits that have already been pushed to a shared repository unless rewriting history is intentional.

docs.title: Revert vs Reset
docs.text:
The key distinction is whether you want to preserve or rewrite history.

Goal Command History Undo a shared commit git revert <commit> Preserves history Move branch back locally git reset <commit> Rewrites branch history Undo and keep changes staged git reset --soft <commit> Rewrites branch history Undo and keep changes unstaged git reset --mixed <commit> Rewrites branch history Undo and discard changes git reset --hard <commit> Rewrites branch history

Rule of thumb

Already pushed/shared? Prefer:

git revert <commit>

Local and not shared? git reset may be appropriate.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Situation Command Show current HEAD git rev-parse HEAD Show short HEAD git rev-parse --short HEAD Find commits git log --oneline Discard file changes git restore <file> Unstage file git restore --staged <file> Undo shared commit git revert <commit> Move branch to a commit git reset <commit> Move branch and keep changes staged git reset --soft <commit> Move branch and keep changes unstaged git reset --mixed <commit> Move branch and discard changes git reset --hard <commit> Reset to previous commit git reset --hard HEAD~1 Reset working tree to HEAD git reset --hard HEAD

docs.title: 1.1 Loading a Project
docs.text:
1. Open VSCode.
  2. Go to File -> Open Folder and select your project folder.
  3. VSCode will automatically detect if it's a Git repository.

docs.title: 1.2 Git Panel
docs.text:
• Click the Source Control icon on the left sidebar (or Ctrl+Shift+G).
  • You can see modified files, staged files, and commit history.

docs.title: 1.3 Basic Operations in VSCode
docs.text:
• Stage Changes: Click + next to files or Stage All Changes.
  • Commit Changes: Enter a commit message and click the checkmark ✔.
  • Push/Pull:
  • Click the ... menu in the Source Control panel.
  • Select Push to upload commits to remote.
  • Select Pull to fetch changes from remote.

docs.title: 1.4 Cloning a Repository in VSCode

1. Press Ctrl+Shift+P (or Cmd+Shift+P on macOS) to open the command palette.
  2. Type Git: Clone and select it.
  3. Enter the repository URL.
  4. Select a local folder for the cloned project.
