docs.title: 1.5 Extensions for Git
docs.text:
• GitLens – advanced Git insights and history tracking.
  • Git Graph – visual representation of branches and commits.

docs.title: Basic Feature Workflow
docs.text:
Start from the latest main:

git switch main
git pull

Create a feature branch:

git switch -c feature/my-feature

Make changes and stage them:

git add .

Commit:

git commit -m "Add my feature"

Push the branch:

git push -u origin feature/my-feature

Create a merge/pull request through your Git hosting platform.

docs.title: Typical Workflow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[main] --> B[Create feature branch]
    B --> C[Make changes]
    C --> D[git add]
    D --> E[git commit]
    E --> F[git push]
    F --> G[Merge/Pull Request]
    G --> A

docs.title: Keep a Feature Branch Updated
docs.text:
Update local main:

git switch main
git pull

Return to the feature branch:

git switch feature/my-feature

Merge the updated main:

git merge main

Alternatively, rebase:

git rebase main

Warning

Rebasing rewrites commit history. Avoid rebasing commits that have already been pushed and are being used by other developers unless your team workflow explicitly allows it.

docs.title: Conventional Commit Messages
docs.text:
A common convention is:

type(scope): description

Examples:

feat(api): add authentication endpoint
fix(auth): handle expired tokens
docs(git): add branching guide
refactor(cli): simplify argument parsing
test(api): add integration tests
chore(deps): update dependencies

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
uv is a fast Python package and project manager developed by Astral.

It can manage:

  • Python installations
  • Virtual environments
  • Project dependencies
  • Lockfiles
  • Python project metadata
  • Command execution
  • Python tools
  • Package builds
  • Workspaces

Unlike traditional workflows that combine python, venv, pip, pip-tools, and pyenv, uv can provide most of these capabilities through a single tool.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Platform Command Ubuntu / Debian curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh \| sh Fedora curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh \| sh Arch curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh \| sh macOS brew install uv Windows winget install --id=astral-sh.uv -e

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Task Command uv version uv --version uv location which uv Windows location where.exe uv Help uv --help

docs.title: Project
docs.text: Task Command Virtual environment uv venv Create project uv init <name> Initialize current directory uv init Sync environment uv sync Run command uv run <command> Run Python uv run python Show dependency tree uv tree Check lockfile uv lock --check

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Task Command Add dependency uv add <package> Add exact version uv add "<package>==<version>" Add dev dependency uv add --dev <package> Remove dependency uv remove <package> Update all uv lock --upgrade Update one uv lock --upgrade-package <package> Update to version uv lock --upgrade-package "<package>==<version>" Synchronize uv sync

docs.title: Python
docs.text: Task Command List Python versions uv python list List installed versions uv python list --only-installed Install Python uv python install 3.12 Install multiple versions uv python install 3.11 3.12 3.13 Select project Python uv python pin 3.12 Synchronize environment uv sync Verify project Python uv run python --version

docs.title: Typical Workflow
docs.text:
# Create project
uv init my-project

cd my-project

# Select Python
uv python install 3.12
uv python pin 3.12

# Add dependencies
uv add requests
uv add --dev pytest ruff

# Create/sync environment
uv sync

# Run application
uv run python main.py

# Run tests
uv run pytest

# Check code
uv run ruff check .

# Update dependencies
uv lock --upgrade
uv sync

# Commit project configuration
git add pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version
git commit -m "Update Python dependencies"
git push

Recommended project files

For a typical uv-managed Python project, commit:

pyproject.toml
uv.lock
.python-version

and exclude:

.venv/

This gives other developers and CI enough information to recreate the project's Python environment without committing the environment itself.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: uv can be installed without having Python or Rust installed first. The official standalone installer is the recommended cross-platform approach, while package managers are also available.

docs.title: Ubuntu / Debian
docs.text:
The most portable option is the official installer:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

If curl isn't available:

wget -qO- https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Restart your shell after installation if required.

source ~/.bashrc

or:

source ~/.zshrc

Note

The official installer may modify your shell profile so that the `uv` executable is available on your `PATH`.

docs.title: Fedora
docs.text:
You can use the official installer:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Or, if uv is available through your configured Fedora repositories:

sudo dnf install uv

Verify:

uv --version

docs.title: Arch Linux
docs.text:
If uv is available in your configured Arch repositories:

sudo pacman -S uv

Alternatively, use the official installer:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

docs.title: Homebrew
docs.text:
If Homebrew is installed:

brew install uv

Verify:

uv --version

The official uv documentation lists Homebrew as a supported installation method.

docs.title: Standalone Installer
docs.text:
Alternatively:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

docs.title: WinGet
docs.text:
Using Windows Package Manager:

winget install --id=astral-sh.uv -e

Then open a new terminal and verify:

uv --version

GitHub-style PowerShell installation can also be performed using the official installer:

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

Both methods are documented by the uv project.

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
Regardless of operating system:

uv --version

Example:

uv 0.x.x

Check where the executable is located:

Linux/macOS:

which uv

Windows:

where.exe uv

Display help:

uv --help

Display help for a specific command:

uv help add

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text:
uv's recommended project workflow is based around:

pyproject.toml
uv.lock
.venv/
.python-version

The important distinction is:

pyproject.toml
    │
    ├── Project metadata
    ├── Python requirement
    └── Dependency requirements
              │
              ▼
          uv.lock
              │
              ▼
           .venv/

pyproject.toml describes the project and its dependency requirements.

uv.lock records the exact resolved dependency versions.

.venv contains the project's isolated Python environment.

.python-version can specify the Python version used by the project.

docs.title: Initialize a Project
docs.text:
Create a virtual environment:

uv venv

Create a new project:

uv init my-project

Enter the project:

cd my-project

The project will contain files such as:

my-project/
├── .python-version
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
└── src/
    └── my_project/
        └── __init__.py

uv's default project initialization creates an application-style project.

You can also initialize a project in the current directory:

mkdir my-project
cd my-project

uv init

docs.title: Project Environment
docs.text:
uv automatically manages a virtual environment for the project:

my-project/
├── .venv/
├── pyproject.toml
└── uv.lock

The .venv directory is isolated from the system Python installation.

It should not be committed to Git.

uv automatically creates the environment when required by commands such as uv run or uv sync.

You can explicitly create/synchronize it:

uv sync

docs.title: Running Python
docs.text:
Instead of manually activating the environment, uv can execute commands inside the project environment:

uv run python

Run a script:

uv run python main.py

Run a module:

uv run python -m my_project

Check the Python version being used:

uv run python --version

This is useful because uv run ensures the project environment is up to date before running the command.

docs.title: Activating the Environment
docs.text: You can also activate .venv manually.

docs.title: Linux / macOS
docs.text: source .venv/bin/activate

docs.title: Windows PowerShell
docs.text: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

docs.title: Windows CMD
docs.text:
.venv\Scripts\activate

After activation:

python --version

and:

which python

Linux/macOS should point into:

.venv/bin/python

Windows:

.venv\Scripts\python.exe

Tip

You don't have to activate the environment when using uv.

This:

uv run python main.py

is often preferable to:

source .venv/bin/activate
python main.py

docs.title: Add a Dependency
docs.text:
Add a package:

uv add requests

This updates:

pyproject.toml
uv.lock
.venv/

uv resolves the dependency, updates the lockfile, and synchronizes the environment.

docs.title: Add a Specific Version
docs.text: uv add "requests==2.32.4"

docs.title: Add a Version Constraint
docs.text: uv add "requests>=2.30,<3"

docs.title: Add a Development Dependency
docs.text:
For development-only dependencies:

uv add --dev pytest

For example:

uv add --dev ruff
uv add --dev pytest
uv add --dev mypy

Development dependencies are stored in dependency groups rather than normal runtime dependencies.

docs.title: Remove Dependencies
docs.text:
Remove a dependency:

uv remove requests

Remove a development dependency:

uv remove pytest

uv updates the project configuration, lockfile, and environment.

docs.title: Install / Synchronize Dependencies
docs.text:
Synchronize the project:

uv sync

This installs the dependencies described by the lockfile.

It also removes packages that are no longer part of the locked environment by default.

A useful workflow after cloning a repository is:

git clone <repository>
cd <repository>

uv sync

docs.title: Update Dependencies
docs.text:
Update all dependencies:

uv lock --upgrade

Then synchronize:

uv sync

You can also combine the operations:

uv sync --upgrade

Update a specific dependency:

uv lock --upgrade-package requests

Then:

uv sync

Or update a package to a specific version:

uv lock --upgrade-package "requests==2.32.4"

Dependency upgrades remain constrained by the version requirements declared by the project.

docs.title: Dependency Categories
docs.text:
A typical project might contain:

Runtime dependencies
├── requests
├── fastapi
└── pydantic

Development dependencies
├── pytest
├── ruff
└── mypy

Add runtime dependencies:

uv add requests

Add development dependencies:

uv add --dev pytest
uv add --dev ruff

Install only development dependencies:

uv sync --only-dev

Skip development dependencies:

uv sync --no-dev

uv supports dependency groups for separating development tooling from runtime requirements.

docs.title: Inspect Dependencies
docs.text:
Show the dependency tree:

uv tree

Check the project's configuration:

uv version

Check the lockfile:

uv lock --check

The --check option verifies that the lockfile is up to date without modifying it.

docs.title: Install a Specific Python Version
docs.text:
Install Python 3.12:

uv python install 3.12

Install a specific patch release:

uv python install 3.12.3

Install multiple versions:

uv python install 3.11 3.12 3.13

uv keeps these Python installations separate from the system Python installation.

docs.title: Select the Python Version for a Project
docs.text:
Inside your project:

uv python pin 3.12

This creates:

.python-version

containing the selected Python version.

Example:

3.12

uv uses this file to determine the project's default Python version.

Then recreate/synchronize the environment:

uv sync

Verify:

uv run python --version

Example:

Python 3.12.x

The project is now using its own Python environment:

System Python
     │
     ├── /usr/bin/python3
     │
     └── unaffected

uv-managed Python
     │
     └── Python 3.12
             │
             ▼
          .venv/

docs.title: Change the Python Version
docs.text:
Suppose the project currently uses:

Python 3.12

and you want Python 3.13.

First install the version if necessary:

uv python install 3.13

Pin the project:

uv python pin 3.13

Synchronize the environment:

uv sync

Verify:

uv run python --version

You should now see:

Python 3.13.x

docs.title: Downgrade Python
docs.text:
The same process works in reverse.

For example, change from Python 3.13 to Python 3.12:

uv python install 3.12
uv python pin 3.12
uv sync

Verify:

uv run python --version

The system Python is not changed.

Project-level Python version

The important distinction is:

uv python install 3.12

installs a Python version managed by uv.

While:

uv python pin 3.12

tells a particular project which Python version to use.

Then:

uv sync

synchronizes the project's .venv with that configuration.

docs.title: Python Version Requirements
docs.text:
A project can also specify the Python versions it supports through pyproject.toml.

For example:

[project]
requires-python = ">=3.12"

Or:

[project]
requires-python = ">=3.12,<3.14"

This is different from .python-version.

docs.title: .python-version
docs.text:
Specifies the project's preferred Python version.

3.12

docs.title: requires-python
docs.text:
Specifies which Python versions the project supports.

requires-python = ">=3.12,<3.14"

Think of it as:

.python-version
    │
    └── "Use this Python by default"

requires-python
    │
    └── "These Python versions are supported"

uv uses both when resolving and running the project.

docs.title: Updating uv
docs.text:
If uv was installed using the standalone installer:

uv self update

If installed through a package manager, update it through that package manager.

Example:

docs.title: Linux (Ubuntu)
docs.text: uv self update

docs.title: pip manager
docs.text: python3 -m pip install --upgrade uv

docs.title: pipx manager
docs.text: pipx upgrade uv

docs.title: Homebrew
docs.text: brew upgrade uv

docs.title: WinGet
docs.text:
winget upgrade --id=astral-sh.uv -e

The standalone install supports uv self update; package-manager installations should generally be updated through their package manager.

docs.title: uv and Docker
docs.text:
uv can be used directly inside Docker images.

A simple example:

FROM python:3.12-slim

COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:latest /uv /uvx /bin/

WORKDIR /app

COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./

RUN uv sync --locked --no-install-project

COPY . .

RUN uv sync --locked

CMD ["uv", "run", "my-app"]

The important files are:

pyproject.toml
uv.lock

These should be copied before the rest of the source code where possible so Docker can cache the dependency installation layer.

Danger

Do not copy your local .venv into a Docker image.

A virtual environment is platform-specific. The Docker image should create its own environment. Add .venv to .dockerignore.

Example .dockerignore:

.venv/
.git/
__pycache__/
*.pyc

docs.title: uv and Git
docs.text:
uv works very well with Git because the important project files are text-based and should be committed:

project/
├── pyproject.toml
├── uv.lock
├── .python-version
├── .gitignore
├── README.md
└── src/

Do not commit:

.venv/

A typical .gitignore:

.venv/
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
.pytest_cache/
.mypy_cache/
.ruff_cache/

Commit the lockfile

uv.lock should normally be committed to Git.

It provides reproducible dependency resolution across machines and CI environments.

Typical workflow:

uv add requests

git status

git add pyproject.toml uv.lock

git commit -m "Add requests dependency"

git push

On another machine:

git pull

uv sync

The second machine will recreate the project environment from the project configuration and lockfile.

docs.title: uv and Makefile
docs.text:
uv works well with Makefiles because Make can provide short aliases for common uv commands.

Example:

install:
    uv sync

run:
    uv run python main.py

test:
    uv run pytest

lint:
    uv run ruff check .

format:
    uv run ruff format .

update:
    uv lock --upgrade
    uv sync

clean:
    rm -rf .venv

Then instead of remembering:

uv run pytest

you can use:

make test

Or:

make install
make test
make lint
make format

A useful project workflow becomes:

Makefile
   │
   ├── install ──► uv sync
   ├── test ─────► uv run pytest
   ├── lint ─────► uv run ruff
   └── run ──────► uv run ...

This is particularly useful in teams because developers and CI can use the same commands.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
These tools work well together:

                 Git Repository
                       │
          ┌────────────┴────────────┐
          │                         │
   pyproject.toml                uv.lock
          │                         │
          └──────────┬──────────────┘
                     │
                    uv
                     │
                  .venv
                     │
          ┌──────────┴──────────┐
          │                     │
       Makefile              Dockerfile
          │                     │
          │                     │
     local commands        container build

A typical development workflow:

git clone <repository>

cd project

uv sync

make test

make lint

git add .

git commit -m "Implement feature"

git push

CI/CD can then use the same dependency definition:

uv sync --locked
uv run pytest

Docker can use:

uv sync --locked

This gives you one source of truth for Python dependencies: pyproject.toml plus uv.lock.
